newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, soybean prices soar on strike worries.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, soybean prices soar on strike worries.

text.p: Coffee prices soared to the highest level in two years and and soybeans also rose Monday as Brazilian dockworkers prepared for a strike that could cripple exports of Brazil's most valuable crops.

Comments by a U.S. Agriculture Department official over the weekend, hinting that global coffee supplies may be tighter than previously estimated, and a Merrill Lynch prediction of a 20-year low in Colombian coffee production, also boosted prices.

The planned dockworkers strike at Brazil's Parangua port was set for Wednesday, and longshoremen at other ports where the bulk of Brazil's coffee crop is exported may join the strike in sympathy. Brazil is the world's largest producer.
Officials from the local dockworkers' union said Parangua's port was already operating at half its normal capacity, but traders and port officials disputed the claim.

Coffee for May delivery jumped 8 cents to 184.85 cents a pound at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, the highest level for the most active contract since March 1995. The spot March contract rose 8.05 cents to 198.45 cents, at one point eclipsing the widely watched $2 a pound mark.

"From a technical point of view, it's a very bullish market," said Albert Scalla of Hencorp Becstone in Miami. "There is a marked lack of selling by origins ... and some of the statements made by the USDA also helped."

U.S. Department of Agriculture coffee analyst Edmond Missiaen, speaking at an industry conference on Saturday, said this year's global coffee production may turn out to be lower than the 100.9 million 132-pound bags forecast in December.

"I would guess the next revision is more likely to be down than up," Missiaen said at the National Coffee Association's annual meeting in Scottsdale, Arizona. The next U.S. government estimate is scheduled for mid-June.

Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes, writing in a report, forecast this year's coffee crop in Colombia, the world's second-biggest producer, would be between 9.4 million and 10.5 million bags -- a 20-year low.
A recent Colombian government assessment that the country would produce 10.4 million bags, compared to 12.9 million last year, has set off a buying frenzy in the futures markets.
"The prospect of a vastly reduced Colombian crop at a time when Central American production is also falling below expectations should keep a strong upward bias to the market," Ganes' report said.

Coffee prices have risen by more than 50 percent since the start of the year, as market participants reacted to steadily declining domestic stockpiles and signs of lower production in key countries like Colombia.
Meanwhile soybean prices leaped to a five-month high.
"If (Brazilian dockworkers) happen to strike for a long time, we're going to have to ration beans," said one trader.
World and U.S. supplies of soybeans are very low so any supply disruption could cause wild price fluctuations.
March soybeans hit a high of $8.12 a bushel, equalling the high set Sept. 23, 1996. The contract closed up 14 cents at $8.05 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Excessive rains in northern Brazil, which could delay soybean harvesting and damage the maturing corn crop, also gave the market a boost, Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. said.
March corn rose 6 cents to $3.02-3/4 a bushel.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 commodity futures rose 1.16 points to 243.57.
April gold fell $1.30 to $363.80 an ounce and May silver sank 2 cents to $5.34 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, April platinum fell $4.60 to $391.80 an ounce, while concerns about Russia's palladium mining operations lifted June palladium $1.25 to $156.30 an ounce.

Workers at Russia's big Norilsk mine gave management a 10-day deadline to meet back demands but management said it could not meet the deadline. Workers have threatened to strike beginning on March 15.
Russia is the world's main supplier of palladium and the second-largest supplier of platinum.
Oil prices ended lower but recovered from a drop below $20 a barrel. It was the first time prices had dropped below the key $20 level since June 26 when the spot contract fell to $19.85.

April crude fell 5 cents to $20.25 a barrel. April heating oil fell 0.26 cent to 53.18 cents a gallon, shrugging off forecasts for a bout of colder weather for the Northeast. April gasoline sank 0.79 cent to 61.77 cents a gallon.
